render.title: How DNP uncouples the proton gradient from ATP synthesis
render.body:
2,4-Dinitrophenol (DNP) is a small, lipid-soluble molecule that acts as a proton carrier — it can pick up a proton (H+) on one side of the inner mitochondrial membrane and carry it to the other side, bypassing ATP synthase entirely.

Here is what normally happens: the electron transport chain pumps protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space, building up a proton gradient. Protons can only get back into the matrix through ATP synthase, so as they flow through it, ATP is made. The gradient and ATP synthesis are tightly coupled.

DNP breaks that coupling. Because DNP is hydrophobic, it dissolves into the inner membrane, picks up a proton in the intermembrane space (where proton concentration is high), and diffuses across to the matrix side, where it releases the proton. It then cycles back and picks up another one. Protons flood back into the matrix without ever passing through ATP synthase, so the energy stored in the gradient is released as heat rather than used to make ATP.

Why does oxygen consumption increase? The electron transport chain keeps pumping protons as fast as electrons flow through it. Normally, a build-up of the proton gradient eventually slows the chain (backpressure). DNP drains the gradient continuously, so the backpressure never builds — the chain runs at full speed and burns through oxygen at a higher rate. More oxygen consumed, but the ATP output drops sharply because the proton flow no longer drives ATP synthase.

The net result is that cellular respiration becomes very inefficient: chemical energy from glucose is wasted as heat. This is why DNP was briefly used as a weight-loss drug in the 1930s — it burns calories without producing useful ATP. However, the effect is dose-dependent and uncontrollable, and it caused fatal hyperthermia in several users.
render.summary: DNP is a lipid-soluble proton carrier that shuttles H+ across the inner mitochondrial membrane without going through ATP synthase. This collapses the proton gradient, so its energy is released as heat rather than ATP. The electron transport chain loses its backpressure and runs faster, consuming more oxygen, while ATP output falls sharply.
